name: Treaty at camp in Scott's Valley (1851), unratified California treaty R
aka: Treaty R of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 4 set apart as an Indian reservation, its use and possession 'forever guarantied' to the signing tribes and to other tribes the United States might move there from the Klamath and Trinity rivers, a tract around Scott's valley and across the Klamath to the 42nd parallel, estimated at twenty-four miles by fifteen.

Article 4 let miners already working that part of Scott's river keep their claims for two years and let settlers stay until June 1, 1852, and reserved to the United States a right of way and the use of up to one thousand acres for farming.

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty R in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States Senate, executive session; record reprinted 1905

source.title: Robert F. Heizer, The Eighteen Unratified Treaties of 1851-1852 between the California Indians and the United States Government (1972)
source.publisher: Archaeological Research Facility, University of California, Berkeley

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

source.title: Act of May 18, 1928, ch. 624, 45 Stat. 602 (Indians of California jurisdictional act)

breaches.quote: the loss to the said Indians on account of their failure to secure the lands and compensation provided for in the eighteen unratified treaties

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 305, 306 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's history says twelve Shasta headmen signed Treaty R on November 4, 1851, while settlers were preparing a war of extermination against them, that the California legislature lobbied Congress against the reservations, that the Senate, acting largely on local complaints, rejected the treaties in 1852 and kept them secret until 1905, and that California funded militia campaigns against the tribes of Siskiyou, Modoc and Shasta counties from 1852 to 1856.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: Klamath Tribes, Oregon.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.

Heizer (1972) prints only Article 4 of this treaty, so the relinquishment article and the goods, mechanics and teachers promised were not checked; because the Senate rejected the treaty, the United States took the land without the reserved tract or the promised goods (1928 Act, section 2).

Heizer's printed heading for this treaty reads 'October 6, 1851', but its closing clause, the President's schedule and the 1852 message all give November 4, 1851; the heading appears to repeat treaty Q's date.

The Senate's rejection date is given as July 8, 1852 by Heizer (1972, introduction), but the Senate clerk's 1904 search quoted in the National Archives' Prologue article (2013) gives July 2, 1852; the Senate Executive Journal was not opened to settle it.

Audit 2026-11-08: promises rewritten from treaty R's own text (Heizer 1972); the four generic promises copied across the California files ('Article 3 or 4', beef and flour 'during 1851 and 1852', staff 'for at least five years') did not fit this treaty or could not be checked for it.
